title: The Gang Beats Boggs: Ladies Reboot

jokes.text: Wade Boggs. He's a Hall of Fame baseball guy who drank 70 beers on a cross-country flight. We're gonna beat that record. That's why I booked us these tickets. Uh, I thought we were flying to Los Angeles for the Women's March.
jokes.setup: Dee announces she booked tickets to the Women's March, implying feminist purpose
jokes.punchline: The actual reason is to beat a man's beer-drinking record — a deeply anti-feminist motivation disguised in feminist packaging
jokes.explanation: Strong premise setup — the irony that an all-female trip to the Women's March is actually about copying a man's record is a sharp, character-specific joke. Only Dee would frame this self-delusion so earnestly. Sets the episode's central comedic tension efficiently.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Wade Boggs. He's a Hall of Fame baseball guy who drank 70 beers on a cross-country flight. We're gonna beat that record.

jokes.text: I didn't know it was an all-female flight. That feels dangerous.
jokes.setup: The group discusses the all-female flight
jokes.punchline: Mrs. Mac's reflexive sexism — finding an all-female flight inherently dangerous — delivered deadpan
jokes.explanation: Perfectly economical. Mrs. Mac's internalized misogyny expressed with complete sincerity is a good character joke. The brevity is the craft — four words do the heavy lifting. Character-specific without being overplayed.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I didn't know it was an all-female flight. That feels dangerous.

jokes.text: Can't smoke on an airplane. Goddamn, when's the last time you flew?
jokes.setup: Someone tries to light a cigarette on the plane
jokes.punchline: The question 'when's the last time you flew?' implies this person is so out of touch they forgot planes banned smoking decades ago
jokes.explanation: Functional gag about how insulated these characters are from normal life. Competent but not particularly inventive — the joke is fairly predictable once the cigarette appears.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Can't smoke on an airplane. Goddamn, when's the last time you flew?

jokes.text: It's the same exact thing, but it's with women. Right? So it's a new idea.
jokes.setup: Artemis pushes back on copying the guys' beer challenge exactly
jokes.punchline: Dee's earnest defense of a 'female reboot' being inherently new just because women do it — a meta-commentary on lazy Hollywood reboots
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's thesis joke and it's genuinely excellent. The show is openly criticizing the 'gender-swap reboot' trend (and self-criticizing, since this episode IS that trope) in a single, perfectly economical line. It's self-aware without being smug, and Dee delivers it with complete sincerity, which makes it sharper. Among the best craft moments in the episode — comparable to the 8.0 anchor in its economy and layered meaning.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: It's the same exact thing, but it's with women. Right? So it's a new idea.

jokes.text: Judy Garland, Liz Taylor... Joan Crawford... Betty Ford! / Those are all sad examples of alcohol abuse.
jokes.setup: Artemis suggests they should beat a female record-holder's drinking feat instead of Boggs
jokes.punchline: Every female drinking 'icon' she names is actually a tragic alcoholic — Dee correctly points out they're all sad cautionary tales, not celebration-worthy records
jokes.explanation: The escalating list of tragic female drinkers — culminating in Betty Ford, who literally founded a rehab clinic — is well-constructed dark comedy. The structure is solid: each name is funnier than the last, with Betty Ford as a perfect cap. Dee's deflation of it is the right punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Like some badass woman who could really throw them back? You know, Judy Garland, Liz Taylor... Joan Crawford... Betty Ford!

jokes.text: When women do it, it just feels sad.
jokes.setup: Discussion about whether beating Boggs's record is fun or depressing for women
jokes.punchline: Dee, a woman, calmly agrees that women drinking competitively just feels sad — undercutting her own empowerment premise
jokes.explanation: Economical and darkly self-aware. The joke works because Dee doesn't even argue — she just absorbs the insult and pivots. It's very Sunny in its nihilism. Short, landing in one breath.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Those are all sad examples of alcohol abuse. The Boggs thing just feels more fun, you know? When women do it, it just feels sad.

jokes.text: Okay. So, last time, Mac was commissioner, but I figured I could do that and participate because women are excellent multitaskers.
jokes.setup: Dee explains her organizational plan for the challenge
jokes.punchline: She invokes the 'women are great multitaskers' cliché as genuine reasoning, obliviously leaning into the trope she's supposed to be subverting
jokes.explanation: Decent character moment — Dee using a gender stereotype to justify her plan is funny but a bit predictable. Works as texture more than a standalone joke.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Last time, Mac was commissioner, but I figured I could do that and participate because women are excellent multitaskers.

jokes.text: How come the coloreds are allowed to sit up front with the whites and we're way back here?
jokes.setup: Mrs. Mac is confused about the seating arrangement on the plane
jokes.punchline: She interprets the first-class/coach divide through a horrifying racial lens, revealing the depth of her ignorance and prejudice
jokes.explanation: Deeply character-specific and shocking — Mrs. Mac's racism and obliviousness are her defining traits. The recontextualization of airplane class as a racial system is audacious. Loses points on 'earned vs. cheap' because the joke leans on the shock of the slur more than structural wit. The immediate reaction 'Wow. I never heard you talk so much. Truly awful.' is a good straight-man landing.

dialogue.speaker: Mrs. Mac
dialogue.line: How come the coloreds are allowed to sit up front with the whites and we're way back here?

jokes.text: Wow. I never heard you talk so much. Truly awful.
jokes.setup: Mrs. Mac delivers her racist airplane observation
jokes.punchline: Dee's reaction conflates the quantity of speech with its content — she's as horrified by Mrs. Mac talking as by what she said
jokes.explanation: Smart double-layered reaction. 'Truly awful' is pitch-perfect — it works as both a critique of the racism AND an observation that Mrs. Mac rarely speaks. Good economy, good structure.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Wow. I never heard you talk so much. Truly awful.

jokes.text: She ate all her nicotine patches already. Ate them?! What? You're not supposed to eat them. Oh, my God, there was a two-week supply.
jokes.setup: Someone asks why Mrs. Mac is so hyper/perky
jokes.punchline: She consumed a two-week supply of nicotine patches orally, which would constitute a near-toxic dose — her perkiness is nicotine poisoning
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'ate patches' to 'two-week supply' is well-timed. This is good Sunny absurdism — a mundane health aid turned into self-poisoning. The beat lands because the horror escalates naturally in the dialogue.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: She ate all her nicotine patches already.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Ate them?! What? You're not supposed to eat them.

jokes.text: In that case, since you're all hopped up, you be the commissioner.
jokes.setup: Mrs. Mac is on a nicotine overdose high
jokes.punchline: Dee's pragmatic response is to put the drug-addled person in charge of bookkeeping
jokes.explanation: Functional gang logic — their solution to someone being impaired is to give them responsibility. Competent but not outstanding.

dialogue.speaker: Mrs. Mac
dialogue.line: Oh, no. Two women pilots. I'm getting out of here.

jokes.text: Oh, no. Two women pilots. I'm getting out of here.
jokes.setup: The female pilots make a welcome announcement
jokes.punchline: Mrs. Mac's immediate terror at women flying the plane — mid-flight — and her attempt to literally leave
jokes.explanation: Perfectly in character for Mrs. Mac, whose internalized sexism has been established. The physical absurdity of trying to exit a plane in mid-air elevates it beyond a simple bigotry joke. 'I'm getting out of here' on an airplane is a great escalation of her earlier 'that feels dangerous' line.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: We're in mid-goddamn-air. You know what? Drink your beer. That'll calm your nerves.

jokes.text: Drink your beer. That'll calm your nerves.
jokes.setup: Mrs. Mac is panicking about women pilots
jokes.punchline: Dee's solution to panic is to advance the alcohol challenge — perfectly merging her two agendas
jokes.explanation: Quick, efficient joke. Dee's single-mindedness about the challenge bleeding into her crisis management is a solid character beat.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Why do women pee so much?

jokes.text: Keep going like that, we might have ourselves a real scrimmage. She's gonna be passed out by Indiana. Just mark her shirt off while she's still in the game.
jokes.setup: Mrs. Mac is drinking wildly on her nicotine high
jokes.punchline: Dee reduces her friend's likely alcohol poisoning to sports analytics — 'mark her shirt while she's still in the game' treats passing out as a scoring opportunity
jokes.explanation: Good Sunny nihilism — Dee treating a friend's impending unconsciousness as a tactical sports consideration. 'While she's still in the game' is the killer phrase, using sports language for something genuinely dangerous.

dialogue.speaker: The Waitress
dialogue.line: I'm an alcoholic.

jokes.text: Why do women pee so much? / Uh, lady, thank you so much for saving my spot. / I wasn't.
jokes.setup: Dee is impatient in the bathroom line and assumes someone was holding her place
jokes.punchline: The stranger flatly was not saving her spot, combined with Dee's frustrated generalization about women's bathroom habits
jokes.explanation: Two quick jokes layered — Dee's sexist generalization about women followed by a small social humiliation. Neither is exceptional but they work together efficiently.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Secretariat? The racehorse?

jokes.text: Nine, huh? Nine, Waitress. Very nice. I like that. Some record chugging. What's your secret? / I'm an alcoholic. / That'll do it.
jokes.setup: Dee is impressed by Waitress being at 9 drinks and asks her secret
jokes.punchline: Waitress flatly admits she's an alcoholic — not competing, just doing what she does — and Dee accepts this without missing a beat
jokes.explanation: Excellent setup-punchline with perfect economy. The Waitress's alcoholism has been an ongoing character trait across the series, so this lands as a callback for longtime fans while also working cold. 'That'll do it' is a perfect straight-line acceptance. Three words, no waste. The gap between Dee's sports-commentary framing ('record chugging') and the Waitress's clinical self-diagnosis is the joke. Near the top of the episode's craft.

dialogue.speaker: Artemis
dialogue.line: I don't like that she was named after a secretary. She should be a boss.

jokes.text: Secretariat? The racehorse? / I like that. Let's beat a Secretariat. / Mm, I don't like that she was named after a secretary.
jokes.setup: The group wants to find a female athletic record to beat instead of Boggs; someone suggests Secretariat
jokes.punchline: First absurdity: Secretariat is a racehorse. Second absurdity: someone objects to 'her' name being secretary-adjacent, misreading the word entirely
jokes.explanation: Double-layered absurdist escalation — the first joke is suggesting a horse as a drinking role model; the second is feminist indignation at the horse's name based on a misreading. 'She should be a boss' as a rebuttal to a horse's name is good absurdism.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I don't get into this bathroom soon I'm gonna shit my pants!

jokes.text: I don't get into this bathroom soon I'm gonna shit my pants! / Yes! Do it! See? That's what I'm talking about.
jokes.setup: Dee has been arguing that the female reboot should be more shocking than the male version
jokes.punchline: Someone threatens to defecate in their pants, and Dee celebrates this as the groundbreaking female content she's been pitching — gross-out as feminist innovation
jokes.explanation: Smart comedy because Dee's enthusiasm about potential pants-shitting as a feminist achievement recontextualizes it. The joke isn't the gross-out; it's Dee's reaction framing it as subversive art. Good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Yes! Do it! See? That's what I'm talking about. Gross-out humor. It's like taking the original to the next level. Nobody expects that from women. It's so much more shocking, isn't it?

jokes.text: Gross-out humor. It's like taking the original to the next level. See? Nobody expects that from women. It's so much more shocking, isn't it?
jokes.setup: Dee celebrates the potential pants-shitting moment
jokes.punchline: She narrates her own comedic theory about female gross-out humor being inherently more subversive — the show commenting on its own episode-level conceit
jokes.explanation: Meta-layer works well here. Dee is essentially arguing Sunny's own case for why this episode exists, while being completely wrong about its quality. The show is self-aware enough to know this is a bit of a lazy premise.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: They don't check medical bags. See? The guys didn't do that last time. How's that for originality?

jokes.text: I need two more beers. / We're out. / No problemo. I planned for this. [Pulls beers from medical bag]
jokes.setup: The plane runs out of beer and Dee needs more
jokes.punchline: Dee smuggled beers in a medical bag, knowing flight attendants don't check those — revealing forethought that she applies exclusively to drinking challenges
jokes.explanation: Good visual gag with character specificity — Dee's planning abilities are entirely devoted to drinking. The 'they don't check medical bags' detail is clever and specific.

dialogue.speaker: Artemis
dialogue.line: Just, uh, crystals, worry dolls, dream catchers, labia rings... your basics.

jokes.text: See? The guys didn't do that last time. How's that for originality?
jokes.setup: Dee pulls smuggled beers from a medical bag
jokes.punchline: She claims medical-bag beer smuggling as a feminist innovation — still defining originality relative to what men did
jokes.explanation: Callback to the meta-reboot argument — Dee's originality is defined entirely by contrast with men, which undermines her argument. Good thematic consistency.

dialogue.speaker: Artemis
dialogue.line: It's a land of sad, lonely, desperate women willing to pay any price for fake spirituality and clean orgasms.

jokes.text: Where are my beers? / Oh, I had to make room for all my merchandise. Just, uh, crystals, worry dolls, dream catchers, labia rings... your basics.
jokes.setup: Dee discovers her smuggled medical bag beer stash is gone
jokes.punchline: Artemis replaced the beers with crystals, worry dolls, dream catchers, and 'labia rings' — casually described as 'your basics'
jokes.explanation: Perfectly Artemis. The escalating list of wellness products culminating in 'labia rings' as the casual peak item, then immediately normalized with 'your basics,' is excellent list comedy. The casualness of the delivery is what makes 'labia rings' land — it's thrown in as mundane. Strong character integration; this is undeniably Artemis.

dialogue.speaker: Mrs. Mac
dialogue.line: Ooh, I want to... I-I want to 'gasm.

jokes.text: It's a land of sad, lonely, desperate women willing to pay any price for fake spirituality and clean orgasms.
jokes.setup: Artemis explains her California wellness merchandise scheme
jokes.punchline: Her pitch for the California market is essentially a savage indictment of wellness culture — delivered with entrepreneurial enthusiasm
jokes.explanation: Sharp cultural commentary delivered as a business pitch. 'Clean orgasms' is a great absurd detail — specific enough to feel like parody of real products. High quotability because the phrasing is so particular. Very Artemis in its combination of cynicism and enthusiasm.

dialogue.speaker: Flight Attendant
dialogue.line: How do I keep winding up with you people?

jokes.text: Ooh, I want to... I-I want to 'gasm. / See? Lookin' at my first customer.
jokes.setup: Artemis mentions 'clean orgasms' as a product
jokes.punchline: Mrs. Mac's nicotine-addled enthusiasm for orgasms immediately makes her a mark; Artemis recognizes her first victim
jokes.explanation: Good quick beat. Mrs. Mac's hopped-up vulnerability being immediately identified by the predatory Artemis is funny. The 'gasm' truncation from Mrs. Mac feels right for her character.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: How come you're a man servant? Shouldn't there be a woman servant on an all-female flight?

jokes.text: Hey, you! Servant! / Hold on a sec. Servant. / Oh, dear God.
jokes.setup: Dee needs to flag down the male flight attendant
jokes.punchline: She calls him 'servant' twice, with the flight attendant's 'Oh, dear God' reaction implying this is beneath his dignity
jokes.explanation: Quick cringe beat — Dee's classism/obliviousness in calling the flight attendant 'servant.' Functional but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Great. You're a soy boy beta cuck.

jokes.text: I used to work at Guigino's. And then I moved to Minnesota and I waited on you guys at the Super Bowl. / Nothing? Mm? / Nope. / Forget it, forget it, forget it.
jokes.setup: The flight attendant tries to remind the gang who he is
jokes.punchline: The gang has absolutely no memory of him despite apparently memorable encounters — he's completely beneath their notice
jokes.explanation: Meta-callback for fans who saw the original episodes. The joke rewards loyal viewers while also working as a simple 'gang is terrible, doesn't remember service workers' gag. The accumulated pathos of the flight attendant's 'Forget it' is good deflation.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: And you can put it on the Boggs account. Just make sure you keep all the ladies in the white tees lubricated.

jokes.text: Great. You're a soy boy beta cuck. / A what? / Whatever.
jokes.setup: The male flight attendant explains he volunteered for the all-female flight to honor and champion women
jokes.punchline: Dee immediately dismisses his genuine ally behavior with internet-incel terminology, then waves it off — she's using misogynist language to dismiss a feminist ally
jokes.explanation: Layered irony — Dee, who ostensibly organized a feminist trip, uses men's-rights language to dismiss an actual feminist ally. 'A what? / Whatever' is a perfect economic beat on the flight attendant's bewilderment. The hypocrisy is very Sunny.

dialogue.speaker: Flight Attendant
dialogue.line: Uh, in honor of the Women's March, we are serving pink wine. So we only have rosé.

jokes.text: And you can put it on the Boggs account.
jokes.setup: Dee orders 50 beers each from the flight attendant
jokes.punchline: She assumes there's a 'Boggs account' — as if Wade Boggs has a tab running on this airline
jokes.explanation: Quick absurdist throwaway — Dee's total commitment to the Boggs mythology extends to believing there's a standing account for it. Brief but charming.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I just found out Secretariat was a boy. All racehorses are male. I know, because I find them so attractive.

jokes.text: In honor of the Women's March, we are serving pink wine. So we only have rosé.
jokes.setup: Dee orders 50 beers each
jokes.punchline: The all-female feminist flight only serves rosé — a lazy, patronizing gender stereotype dressed up as a tribute
jokes.explanation: Good irony — the feminist flight honors women by serving the most stereotypically 'girly' wine. The well-meaning flight attendant is obliviously sexist. Works as social commentary.

dialogue.speaker: Mrs. Mac
dialogue.line: Pussies on the track.

jokes.text: Cute. Great. Uh, we'll take a shit ton of pink wine. Thank you.
jokes.setup: Dee is confronted with rosé instead of beer
jokes.punchline: After a beat of resigned sarcasm ('Cute. Great.'), she pivots completely and orders in bulk — her commitment to the challenge overrides everything else
jokes.explanation: 'Cute. Great.' is a nice deadpan before the pivot. Dee's single-mindedness is well-expressed.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: I happen to know that tennis great Martina Navratilova drank 70 beers on a flight to L.A., only to wake up the next morning and beat her rival, Chris Evert, at the California Open.

jokes.text: I just found out Secretariat was a boy. All racehorses are male. / I know, because I find them so attractive.
jokes.setup: The group discovers Secretariat, their chosen female role model, is male
jokes.punchline: One character reveals they knew Secretariat was male because they find male racehorses sexually attractive
jokes.explanation: Perfect dark subversion. The factual correction ('all racehorses are male') is the setup for the character to reveal they know this through sexual attraction to horses. The casual delivery of bestiality attraction as incidental information is excellent Sunny darkness. High impact because nobody sees it coming.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: So now we're gonna try to beat Martina Tinatinova...

jokes.text: They can run just as fast as the boy horses. They should march. Pussies on the track. Pussies on the track.
jokes.setup: The group discusses female racehorses not being allowed to race
jokes.punchline: Mrs. Mac, on her nicotine high, turns a vague feminist complaint about horses into an increasingly unhinged chant of 'Pussies on the track'
jokes.explanation: Nicotine-addled Mrs. Mac turning a conversation about racehorses into a chant is very funny escalation. The slippage from feminist argument to unhinged mantra is well-executed. Character-specific to nicotine-overdosed Mrs. Mac specifically.

dialogue.speaker: Artemis
dialogue.line: You can't just change one small specific and call it new.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: I changed three! The wine... the athlete, and the bag!

jokes.text: I happen to know that tennis great Martina Navratilova drank 70 beers on a flight to L.A., only to wake up the next morning and beat her rival, Chris Evert, at the California Open.
jokes.setup: The group wants a female athletic record to aspire to
jokes.punchline: Dee invents an entirely fictional Martina Navratilova drinking record — the 'California Open' doesn't exist, and nothing about this story is real
jokes.explanation: Good payoff setup — the hallucinated Navratilova later explicitly confirms this story is entirely fabricated. The specificity of 'the California Open' sells the lie. Dee's confidence in delivering false history is very much her character.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Oh, dear! Watching a woman do math scares me!

jokes.text: So now we're gonna try to beat Martina Tinatinova... / No, goddamn it!
jokes.setup: Someone tries to repeat Navratilova's name
jokes.punchline: 'Martina Tinatinova' — a completely garbled version of the name — delivered with equal confidence
jokes.explanation: Quick name-mangling gag. Works in the moment but not especially inventive.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Man, it is sad that there are only chicks on this plane 'cause, I mean, I am all horned up.

jokes.text: I changed three! The wine... / We're still copying the men. / ...the athlete, and the bag!
jokes.setup: Artemis says the modified plan still copies the men
jokes.punchline: Dee counts three superficial changes (wine type, athlete name, bag for smuggling) as constituting a genuinely new creative work — the reboots-are-lazy critique in action
jokes.explanation: Strong callback to the episode's central meta-joke. Dee listing three trivial changes as proof of originality perfectly mirrors how lazy reboots work. The overlapping dialogue ('the wine... the athlete... the bag!') as Artemis talks over her adds to the absurdity.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Well, there is a-a male servant.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Oh, yeah? Hot?

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: No.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Soy boy beta cuck.

jokes.text: I will drink anything that you put in front of me. / Well, there you go. Did you hear that? You happy?
jokes.setup: Artemis and Dee argue about wine versus beer
jokes.punchline: The Waitress's statement — 'I will drink anything you put in front of me' — is the alcoholic's credo delivered as a neutral observation; Dee treats it as a victory in the debate
jokes.explanation: Good character beat for Waitress — her lack of preference or discernment about alcohol is a defining trait used well here. Dee co-opting rock-bottom alcoholism as a point in her argument is nicely dark.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: The only way to beat men is by competing against other women.

jokes.text: Oh, dear! Watching a woman do math scares me!
jokes.setup: Dee begins calculating the beer-to-wine ratio
jokes.punchline: Mrs. Mac is terrified by a woman performing math — her sexism now directed at her own group's capability
jokes.explanation: Very economical and character-specific. Mrs. Mac's consistent internalized misogyny applied to her own ally doing arithmetic is a good bit. The exclamatory delivery works well. High quotability due to the absurdity of the specific fear.

dialogue.speaker: Artemis
dialogue.line: And the goddess stone is for putting up your snatch.

jokes.text: So let's just call it an even 29 to win. Good? / Nerd.
jokes.setup: Dee completes her mathematical calculation of wine-to-beer equivalency
jokes.punchline: After the precise, nerdy calculation, all someone can say is 'Nerd' — perfect deflation
jokes.explanation: One-word punchline works as a beat. Not deep comedy but effective pacing tool.

dialogue.speaker: Artemis
dialogue.line: No, it's my special 'uni-tea.' Well, it's selling like hotcakes. It helps your prostate.

jokes.text: Man, it is sad that there are only chicks on this plane 'cause, I mean, I am all horned up. / Well, there is a-a male servant. / No. Soy boy beta cuck.
jokes.setup: Dee laments the lack of male options on the flight for sex
jokes.punchline: The male flight attendant is immediately dismissed using the same 'soy boy beta cuck' label — a callback that now functions as a running characterization
jokes.explanation: Decent callback. The re-use of the label as shorthand is efficient. The irony of Dee using misogynist terminology to dismiss men who support women remains funny.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Women don't have a prostate, goddammit.

dialogue.speaker: Artemis
dialogue.line: Or is that what men want you to believe?

jokes.text: The main reason I picked an all-female flight is because sex is how Dennis lost. / Oh, Dennis? I-I like to hear about Dennis. Tell me more.
jokes.setup: Dee explains her strategy for the all-female flight
jokes.punchline: The Waitress immediately perks up at the mention of Dennis — revealing her unrequited obsession with him — before Dee cuts it off
jokes.explanation: Perfect character beat for the Waitress. Her Dennis fixation is a long-running series joke, and 'I like to hear about Dennis. Tell me more' is a great delivery of that obsession. Character integration is very high — this only works because of the Waitress's established relationship with Dennis.

dialogue.speaker: Artemis
dialogue.line: This Boggs is busted, 'cause I'm doing my own thing now. And it's empowering and communal. Next level shit, right, ladies?

jokes.text: He and Frank, he... they made a side bet, you know. See who could have sex. And then Dennis ended up banging this disgusting person... / Just the one.
jokes.setup: Dee explains Dennis's loss in the original Boggs challenge
jokes.punchline: 'Just the one' — Dee clarifying Dennis only had sex with one person, delivered as if the low count is damning evidence against him
jokes.explanation: Quick and clean. 'Just the one' as a shameful admission is good delivery. The implication that having sex with 'just one person' is Dennis's failure mode is funny given his self-image.

dialogue.speaker: Artemis
dialogue.line: Yeah, six is a yonic number, I'm cool with it.

jokes.text: Well, I'm gonna beat his record. / There's only one man on this flight. / Okay, well, I will figure something out.
jokes.setup: The Waitress wants to beat Dennis's sex record (having sex on a plane)
jokes.punchline: Dee points out there's only one man available; the Waitress's 'I will figure something out' implies she will find a way regardless
jokes.explanation: Good character moment. The Waitress's desperation and her 'I will figure something out' implies she will sleep with Frank (which pays off later). Good foreshadowing as comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I'm posting up. I figure a plane full of broads, there's gonna be a lot of horny women, so I'm like a spider waiting back here to catch some flies.

jokes.text: You're my Chris Evert. You're my rival, okay? The only reason you're here is so that my hatred of you can fuel my desire to beat you. / Okay. Then I'm gonna beat you, you skank. / Yes. That is the spirit. The only way to beat men is by competing against other women.
jokes.setup: Dee explains why she needs a rival on the flight
jokes.punchline: The rival accepts the insult ('skank') enthusiastically, and Dee concludes that 'the only way to beat men is by competing against other women' — an accidental parody of toxic female competition tropes
jokes.explanation: Smart joke. The punchline 'the only way to beat men is by competing against other women' reads as feminist wisdom but is actually an indictment of internalized competition — and the show knows this. The rival happily accepting 'skank' as a term of engagement is good character comedy. Quotable punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: In every reboot you gotta have somebody from the original to make a cameo.

jokes.text: So the rose quartz is a healing gemstone, as well as the lapis lazuli. And the goddess stone is for putting up your snatch.
jokes.setup: Artemis is selling her wellness products to fellow passengers
jokes.punchline: After two legitimately-sounding crystals, 'goddess stone is for putting up your snatch' — delivered with the same clinical salesperson energy as the previous items
jokes.explanation: Excellent list comedy with a perfect escalation. The structure mirrors real wellness product pitches (legitimate-sounding items, then the absurd one) before landing on vaginal insertion with complete composure. Artemis's sales voice makes it funnier. High character integration — this is very specifically Artemis. The '$70, ladies' capper is good.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Want to rumble?

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: No, I don't, but I do want to beat Dennis, so just pop it in.

jokes.text: No, it's my special 'uni-tea.' / Well, it's selling like hotcakes. Drink up, ladies. / It helps your prostate. / Women don't have a prostate, goddammit. / Or is that what men want you to believe?
jokes.setup: Dee discovers Artemis is selling tea instead of drinking
jokes.punchline: Artemis's 'uni-tea' is pitched as helping the prostate; when corrected that women don't have prostates, she pivots to conspiracy theory — 'or is that what men want you to believe?'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The structure is perfect: 'uni-tea' pun, the absurd prostate claim, the factual correction, and then the pivot to patriarchal conspiracy theory as an escape hatch. 'Or is that what men want you to believe?' is exceptionally quotable and captures a specific type of wellness-culture conspiratorial thinking. Artemis is the only character who could deliver this. Near-exceptional craft.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Oh, you better say cheese, buddy, 'cause you're about to go viral.

jokes.text: No, you know what's pathetic? Is this Boggs ladies remake. / Don't do that. / Huh? Yeah, no. I will do that.
jokes.setup: Dee calls Artemis's six drinks pathetic
jokes.punchline: Artemis turns the critique on the entire premise of the episode — calling the ladies' Boggs remake 'pathetic' — and refuses to be stopped from doing so
jokes.explanation: Good meta moment. The show having Artemis be the voice of critique about lazy reboots — right before emphatically doing her own thing — is well-structured. 'I will do that' is a good assertive punch.

dialogue.speaker: Gail
dialogue.line: Heard you were doing the Boggs Soggs lady reboot thing. Did you lose my invitation?

jokes.text: It's empowering and communal. Next level shit, right, ladies? / Not to mention I've already taken these bitches for three hundo, so, what?
jokes.setup: Artemis declares her wellness scheme as empowering
jokes.punchline: The 'empowering communal' framing is immediately revealed as a scam — she's taken $300 from these women — the feminist language as grift cover
jokes.explanation: Good Sunny moment — the gap between feminist empowerment language and grifting women out of their money is very much the show's wheelhouse. 'Three hundo, so, what?' is a good casual admission.

dialogue.speaker: Mrs. Mac
dialogue.line: ♪ When funny little men are walking down the golden road, Rainbows, rainbows and wine... ♪

jokes.text: All right, goddammit, Mrs. Mac, Artemis is out. / Yeah. Out... of this world.
jokes.setup: Dee announces Artemis is out of the drinking challenge
jokes.punchline: Artemis completes Dee's sentence with 'of this world' — refusing to accept the negative framing and turning it into a compliment for herself
jokes.explanation: Quick wordplay beat. Works well in the moment, economical, good Artemis self-regard.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: That's because when women drink, it is depressing and sad.

jokes.text: Yeah, six is a yonic number, I'm cool with it.
jokes.setup: Artemis accepts her count of six drinks as her final tally
jokes.punchline: She recontextualizes six as 'yonic' (relating to the feminine symbol in Tantric philosophy) — a fake spiritual justification for quitting
jokes.explanation: Brilliant economy. 'Yonic' is a real word (the feminine equivalent of phallic), and Artemis using it to spiritually justify her low drink count is perfect character work. Only Artemis would know this word AND use it as a rationalization. Very high character integration score. Surprisingly smart joke tucked into a quick line.

dialogue.speaker: The Waitress
dialogue.line: I had sex in the bathroom with Frank, and now I'm in a shame spiral. I'm gonna drink myself to death.

jokes.text: Where's the goddamn drink slave? Does anybody here do their job?
jokes.setup: Dee is running out of wine and can't find the flight attendant.
jokes.punchline: She calls him 'drink slave' and demands service, completely unaware or unconcerned that this is rude.
jokes.explanation: Dee's casual dehumanization of service workers is a reliable character beat. 'Drink slave' is funny for its confident entitlement.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Martina Navratilova? I never thought you'd give up when you're so close to beating the record.

jokes.text: Oh, hello, Deandra. / Hey. 15, huh? Nice. I underestimated you, champ.
jokes.setup: Dee encounters the flight attendant, who greets her formally
jokes.punchline: Dee immediately looks at his tally-mark shirt and compliments him as if he's a fellow competitor — she can't turn off the challenge mindset
jokes.explanation: Decent beat about Dee's singular focus. The flight attendant being at 15 drinks is a good reveal (he's apparently been drinking on the job), but it's underdeveloped here.

dialogue.speaker: Hallucination Martina
dialogue.line: Now you're imagining me as Lori Petty in A League of Their Own. That was a good female reboot. No, it was its own thing.

jokes.text: Yo! / Frank. What the hell are you doing here? / I'm posting up. I figure a plane full of broads, there's gonna be a lot of horny women, so I'm like a spider waiting back here to catch some flies.
jokes.setup: Dee discovers a stowaway in the back of the plane
jokes.punchline: Frank has hidden himself on the all-female flight specifically to prey on women — describing himself as 'a spider waiting to catch flies'
jokes.explanation: Perfect Frank entrance. The spider/fly metaphor applied to sexual predation on a feminist flight is exactly Frank's energy — completely unashamed, transactional, and darkly funny because of his self-awareness about what he's doing. 'A plane full of broads' as a business opportunity is very Sunny. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Martina
dialogue.line: I never drank 70 beers before winning the California Open. That's not even a real event.

jokes.text: In every reboot you gotta have somebody from the original to make a cameo. / No.
jokes.setup: Dee tells Frank he's not supposed to be here
jokes.punchline: Frank explicitly frames his presence using reboot/Hollywood logic — he knows he's in a reboot and is justifying his inclusion by genre convention
jokes.explanation: One of the best meta jokes in the episode. Frank is operating with full awareness of reboot tropes — he knows he's the legacy character making a cameo in the gender-swap reboot. The fact that Frank is the one to articulate this, while also having a creepy predatory ulterior motive, makes it both smart and gross. High quotability; the specific phrasing mirrors real Hollywood logic.

dialogue.speaker: Gail
dialogue.line: I've been playing the game the whole time. You're one behind me, loser.

jokes.text: Hey. I heard there's a man back here. / Oh. Nope. It's just you. / Want to rumble? / No, I don't, but I do want to beat Dennis, so just pop it in.
jokes.setup: The Waitress, determined to beat Dennis's sex record, seeks out the only man on the flight
jokes.punchline: Frank offers to fight her ('want to rumble?'); she declines violence but immediately accepts sex ('just pop it in') as her motivation to beat Dennis
jokes.explanation: Exceptional joke. The 'want to rumble?' / 'no but just pop it in' exchange is perfectly constructed. Frank offering a fight as a preamble to sex, and the Waitress's 'no' to violence but immediate 'yes' to sex with Frank — specifically motivated by Dennis jealousy — is dark, funny, and deeply character-specific. 'Just pop it in' is an instant quotable. The best single-joke exchange in the episode, comparable to the 8.0 anchor in its economy and character integration, slightly exceeding it in impact.

dialogue.speaker: Artemis
dialogue.line: That tea that I served was spiked with ayahuasca.

jokes.text: I'm gonna need more wine.
jokes.setup: Dee processes the Waitress agreeing to have sex with Frank
jokes.punchline: Dee's only response to this horrifying development is to immediately request more alcohol — the perfect non-reaction reaction
jokes.explanation: Perfect reaction beat. Five words, complete economy, Dee's coping mechanism expressed perfectly. The joke is entirely in what she doesn't say.

dialogue.speaker: Artemis
dialogue.line: It's coming out both ends. The maximum gross-out. So nobody saw that coming from women.

jokes.text: Oh. Okay, so I'm a second-class person? Is that 'cause I'm a woman? Did you hear that, ladies?! / That's not what I said.
jokes.setup: Dee is told she can't go to first class because she's a coach passenger
jokes.punchline: She immediately reframes a class issue as a gender issue — weaponizing feminism to get free first-class access
jokes.explanation: Good Sunny joke about bad-faith feminism. Dee's immediate pivot from class to gender politics, complete with rallying cry to 'ladies!', is a sharp satire of how feminist language gets weaponized for personal gain.

dialogue.line: We're in North Dakota. And only those passengers deemed fit to fly will go on to Los Angeles. And you're not one of them.

jokes.text: Oh, my God! Did you just try and slap me in my face? / No. / Oh, you better say cheese, buddy, 'cause you're about to go viral. Got to connect the Wi-Fi...
jokes.setup: Dee claims the flight attendant tried to slap her (he didn't)
jokes.punchline: She threatens to make him 'go viral' on social media — but then has to pause her outrage to connect to the Wi-Fi first, undermining the spontaneous indignation
jokes.explanation: Smart and contemporary. The 'going viral' threat with the immediate Wi-Fi logistical problem is a perfect deflation of performative outrage culture. Dee's outrage being paused for tech troubleshooting captures the absurdity of the viral justice cycle.

dialogue.line: And only those passengers deemed fit to fly will go on to Los Angeles. And you're not one of them.

jokes.text: [The guys FaceTime in and mock the women's progress, with everyone talking over each other, Dee arguing her wine counts while they claim only 3 beers]
jokes.setup: The men FaceTime in to check on the women's progress
jokes.punchline: Complete chaos — everyone talking over each other, the guys mocking, Dee defending, the wine-to-beer conversion argument devolving — culminating in someone shouting 'Oh, we're all gonna crash!' when the pilots appear
jokes.explanation: The chaos of the FaceTime scene is good situational comedy — the overlapping voices, the argument about wine vs. beer counts, the sudden pilot crisis. Works better as performance than as written jokes. The scene is messier than the sum of its beats.

dialogue.line: Meh.

jokes.text: Snail? / Yeah. Heard you were doing the Boggs Soggs lady reboot thing. Did you lose my invitation?
jokes.setup: Dee discovers another woman in first class has bought all the wine
jokes.punchline: It's 'Snail' — a recurring nemesis — who correctly identifies the episode's premise as 'the Boggs Soggs lady reboot thing' and frames her exclusion as a social slight
jokes.explanation: 'Boggs Soggs lady reboot thing' is a funny name for the episode's premise — casual and deflating. Snail's confident insertion of herself as a victim of exclusion is good character work for a nemesis. The rewatch bonus is for Snail fans.

jokes.text: No. You weren't invited because you're the worst. / Oh, really? 'Cause I'm gonna ruin your game now. Good luck beating the guys. You're stuck at 20, 'cause I bought all the wine.
jokes.setup: Dee and Snail's confrontation
jokes.punchline: Snail has bought ALL the remaining wine, holding Dee's challenge hostage — turning a nemesis relationship into a strategic wine blockade
jokes.explanation: Good plot escalation with character specificity. The nemesis dynamic is well-deployed as a structural obstacle.

jokes.text: I'm gonna salt you, Snail! Back!
jokes.setup: Dee confronts Snail about the wine
jokes.punchline: 'Salt you, Snail' — threatening a snail with the thing that kills snails, as if 'Snail' is her actual nature
jokes.explanation: Genuinely clever. 'I'm gonna salt you, Snail' takes the nickname literally and weaponizes it — threatening the character with what would kill an actual snail. High economy (five words), high originality (the pun is unexpected and logical), and very quotable. One of the cleaner jokes in the episode.

jokes.text: ♪ When funny little men / Are walking down the golden road / Rainbows, rainbows and wine... ♪ / She's gone full Judy Garland. / Isn't it glorious?
jokes.setup: Mrs. Mac, now completely unhinged on nicotine and alcohol, begins singing
jokes.punchline: The reaction 'She's gone full Judy Garland' — the callback to the earlier sad-alcoholic list — lands perfectly as the prediction comes true; someone finds it 'glorious'
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback payoff. The episode foreshadowed this exact fate earlier with the Judy Garland/Liz Taylor/Betty Ford list. Mrs. Mac fulfilling the 'sad women drinking' prophecy while one character finds it glorious and another is horrified is well-structured. The callback gives it extra points — this was set up carefully.

jokes.text: Yeah, I did the mic thing last time and it killed, but when you do it, it just seems to be depressing and sad.
jokes.setup: Mrs. Mac is doing a mic-performing bit while drunk/nicotine-poisoned
jokes.punchline: Dee complains that the same bit she did killed in the men's version but is depressing when women do it — the show's thesis expressed directly
jokes.explanation: Direct statement of the episode's thesis from Dee's perspective. The irony is rich — Dee is criticizing the reboot's failure while being IN the reboot. Good self-awareness from the writers.

jokes.text: That's because when women drink, it is depressing and sad.
jokes.setup: Dee laments that the drinking bit isn't hitting the same way
jokes.punchline: Someone simply and flatly agrees — 'that's because when women drink, it is depressing and sad' — with no irony, confirming the worst reading of the episode
jokes.explanation: Perfect dark capstone on the episode's running gag. The flat, unapologetic delivery of this statement — which the episode has been dancing around since minute one — lands as both the punchline and the thesis. The fact that it's delivered with zero equivocation makes it funnier and more uncomfortable simultaneously.

jokes.text: That's because when women drink, it is depressing and sad.
jokes.setup: Snail says the drinking seems depressing and sad when women do it.
jokes.punchline: Dee accepts the gendered double standard and applies it universally as an explanation — a moment of dark self-awareness that she immediately moves past.
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode. Dee's flat acceptance of the depressing truth — that women drinking is perceived as sad — is both the thesis of the whole episode and a devastating character moment. It crystallizes the gender double standard that's been running all episode in nine words. High economy, strong thematic resonance, good quotability.

jokes.text: I had sex in the bathroom with Frank, and now I'm in a shame spiral.
jokes.setup: The Waitress reappears after her declared intention to find Frank
jokes.punchline: She confirms she went through with it and is now in a shame spiral — the fastest possible consequences for her decision
jokes.explanation: Extremely economical and dark. One sentence delivers the callback payoff, the depravity of the act, and the immediate emotional consequence. 'Shame spiral' is the perfect word for the Waitress's self-awareness about her choices. Among the most quotable lines in the episode. The fact that it's delivered flat, mid-crisis, makes it funnier.

jokes.text: I'm gonna drink myself to death. / Okay, there you go. Whatever keeps you going.
jokes.setup: The Waitress is in a shame spiral after sex with Frank
jokes.punchline: Dee's response to 'I'm gonna drink myself to death' is encouragement — she just needs the Waitress to keep drinking for the challenge
jokes.explanation: Excellent dark beat. 'Whatever keeps you going' as a response to suicidal drinking is perfectly Dee — she's not cruel intentionally, she just doesn't process the gravity of what was said. Very economical, high character integration.

jokes.text: Dennis. / Not Dennis! Don't-don't do... / Don't touch me, okay? Wake up.
jokes.setup: Dee is trying to revive the slumped Waitress
jokes.punchline: The Waitress whispers 'Dennis' in her stupor — her Dennis fixation operating even at her lowest — and Dee's frustrated 'Not Dennis!' shows how tired she is of this
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback. The Waitress is so beaten down — drunk, shamed by Frank sex, possibly dying — and her subconscious is still on Dennis. 'Not Dennis!' from Dee is the right frustrated response. Economical and character-perfect.

jokes.text: Martina Navratilova? / I never thought you'd give up when you're so close to beating the record.
jokes.setup: Dee is despairing about the challenge; she begins hallucinating
jokes.punchline: She hallucinates Martina Navratilova as a motivational coach — the fictional Navratilova of her imagining
jokes.explanation: Good setup for the hallucination sequence. The absurdity of Dee's hallucination being of a person she's completely fabricated is funny in premise.

jokes.text: Chris Evert and I were actually good friends. We'd play a hard match, but then go out for dinner after. Male opponents had the luxury of hating each other. But, as women, we had to stick together to fight for the respect we deserve and grow the sport.
jokes.setup: Hallucinated Martina tries to give Dee genuine feminist wisdom about women in sports
jokes.punchline: Dee stares blankly — she doesn't understand the message at all — the hallucination is trying to teach her something she's incapable of absorbing
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the gap between the genuine wisdom being dispensed and Dee's total inability to receive it. Works as thematic irony but isn't especially funny on its own — more of a structural beat.

jokes.text: You and Chris were... / No. / No. / Okay, I don't get it.
jokes.setup: Martina explains that she and Evert were good friends despite being rivals
jokes.punchline: Dee assumes they were lovers, Martina denies it twice firmly, and Dee admits she simply doesn't understand the actual message about solidarity
jokes.explanation: Economical and funny. Dee's assumption followed by the double denial, then 'I don't get it' — meaning she doesn't understand friendship OR the alternative she was suggesting — is a good quick beat. 'Okay, I don't get it' is very Dee.

jokes.text: No, it's just your imagination filling in the blanks. Really? / Now you're imagining me as Lori Petty in A League of Their Own. / That was a good female reboot. / No, it was its own thing.
jokes.setup: Hallucinated Martina points out she doesn't actually look like this — Dee's imagination is constructing her
jokes.punchline: The hallucination shifts to Dee imagining her as Lori Petty from A League of Their Own; Dee calls that 'a good female reboot'; Martina corrects her — it was its own thing
jokes.explanation: Excellent meta joke. 'That was a good female reboot. No, it was its own thing.' is the episode's thesis distilled into a single exchange — in Dee's hallucination. The show is using an imaginary version of Martina Navratilova to explain the difference between a reboot and an original work, which is exactly what this episode is wrestling with. High originality, strong structure, and very quotable. Near the top of the episode.

jokes.text: And just so you know, I never drank 70 beers before winning the California Open. That's not even a real event. Your whole hallucination is a mess.
jokes.setup: Hallucinated Martina has been Dee's motivational figure for the entire episode
jokes.punchline: The hallucination itself reveals that everything Dee claimed Navratilova did was fabricated — 'your whole hallucination is a mess' is a hallucinated character criticizing the quality of her own hallucination
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. A hallucination debunking itself — 'your whole hallucination is a mess' — is a genuinely original comedic construction. The hallucination is criticizing Dee's poor imagination quality. This is excellent absurdist craft: the logical structure of a hallucination calling itself out for inaccuracy is funny on a conceptual level, and the specific phrase 'your whole hallucination is a mess' is very quotable. Comparable to or slightly exceeding the 8.0 anchor.

jokes.text: Who cares? Tennis is boring.
jokes.setup: Hallucinated Martina has just revealed the entire Navratilova story was fake
jokes.punchline: Dee's response to the collapse of her entire motivational framework is 'who cares, tennis is boring' — instant deflation
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — four words dismiss an entire motivational crisis. Dee's inability to process serious information is well-expressed. Good deflation beat.

jokes.text: Deandra, you should have let them crazy boys do this.
jokes.setup: The hallucination sequence ends with Martina's final verdict
jokes.punchline: Even Dee's hallucination thinks the ladies' Boggs reboot was a bad idea and they should have stayed out of it
jokes.explanation: Good capstone on the hallucination sequence. Dee's subconscious (via imagined Martina) telling her she shouldn't have done this is a nice piece of dramatic irony — she can't even hallucinate support for her own plan.

jokes.text: Deandra, you should have let them crazy boys do this.
jokes.setup: Dee is about to give up on the whole challenge.
jokes.punchline: Even her own hallucination tells her the reboot was a mistake and she should have let the men do it — the ultimate concession from Dee's subconscious.
jokes.explanation: Dee's subconscious literally telling her the episode's premise was wrong is a funny self-critical beat. It's the show being honest about the meta-joke.

jokes.text: I've been playing the game the whole time. You're one behind me, loser. / Snail. / Let's do this.
jokes.setup: Snail approaches the despairing Dee
jokes.punchline: Snail reveals she's been secretly competing this whole time and is ahead of Dee — instantly reigniting Dee's competitive spirit with a single word: 'Snail. Let's do this.'
jokes.explanation: Good character beat. Dee's instant revival at the prospect of defeating a rival is very Sunny — the hatred IS the motivation. 'Snail. Let's do this.' is economical and fun. Good pacing beat for the third act.

jokes.text: Too much spit.
jokes.setup: Dee and Snail are speed-drinking competitively
jokes.punchline: 'Too much spit' — a viscerally gross detail delivered as a clinical assessment mid-chug competition
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — three words, maximum gross-out, delivered with the calm of a sports coach. The specificity of 'too much spit' as the technical flaw in competitive speed-drinking is unexpectedly funny.

jokes.text: Ah, I did it! I did it. I'm Mar-I'm Martina! / It's okay, baby girl. It's over. / I know it's over. 'Cause I beat Martina. I beat Boggs. I'm about to beat all of 'em.
jokes.setup: Dee finishes her 29th bottle of wine and celebrates
jokes.punchline: Artemis says 'It's over' meaning the scheme is being shut down; Dee interprets it as confirmation she beat everyone — a complete misread that reveals her total self-delusion
jokes.explanation: Good classic sitcom misunderstanding but executed with character specificity. Dee's 'I beat Boggs. I'm about to beat all of 'em.' is the peak of her delusion. The structure — Artemis meaning one thing, Dee hearing another — works cleanly.

jokes.text: No. It's over. I'm pulling the plug on your male hand-me-down plot. As women, we deserve better. We deserve our own story.
jokes.setup: Artemis interrupts Dee's celebration
jokes.punchline: Artemis uses the language of feminist empowerment to shut down the challenge — but she's also the character who's been scamming women all episode — the critique and the hypocrisy are both real
jokes.explanation: Good thematic landing. 'Male hand-me-down plot' is a great phrase — applies both to what Dee is doing in-universe and what the show is doing meta-narratively. Artemis as the deliverer of this message, given she's been scamming everyone, is ironic.

jokes.text: That tea that I served was spiked with ayahuasca. / Oh, no! / It's coming out both ends.
jokes.setup: Artemis announces the ayahuasca reveal; chaos ensues
jokes.punchline: 'It's coming out both ends' — the maximum gross-out payoff to the ayahuasca reveal, delivered as a clinical fact
jokes.explanation: Strong payoff on multiple threads. The ayahuasca reveal ties together Artemis's scamming and Dee's earlier stated desire for gross-out female comedy. 'It's coming out both ends' is exactly the kind of maximum gross-out Dee claimed would be groundbreaking — and it's also genuinely funny as a clinical description of what ayahuasca does. Good callback integration.

jokes.text: The maximum gross-out. So nobody saw that coming from women.
jokes.setup: People are having explosive ayahuasca experiences
jokes.punchline: Dee narrates the gross-out as a feminist achievement — she's getting her groundbreaking female gross-out comedy, but it's real vomiting/diarrhea, not performed
jokes.explanation: Good payoff to Dee's earlier gross-out theorizing. She gets exactly what she asked for, in the worst possible way, and celebrates it. 'Nobody saw that coming from women' as a feminist win for real mass ayahuasca poisoning is very dark and very Sunny.

jokes.text: Where are we? / Are we in L.A.? / No. We're in North Dakota. / And only those passengers deemed fit to fly will go on to Los Angeles. And you're not one of them.
jokes.setup: Everyone comes down from ayahuasca chaos
jokes.punchline: They've been diverted to North Dakota — the same fate as Dennis in the original Boggs episode — and Dee specifically is being left behind, mirroring the original's outcome
jokes.explanation: Satisfying structural callback. The reboot ends with the same beat as the original — the character who most embarrassed themselves gets stranded in North Dakota. The irony that Dee's attempt to escape Dennis's fate produces the identical outcome is well-constructed.

jokes.text: Where are we? / Are we in L.A.? / No. We're in North Dakota. And only those passengers deemed fit to fly will go on to Los Angeles. And you're not one of them.
jokes.setup: The plane has made an emergency stop.
jokes.punchline: They've landed in North Dakota — the same place Dennis abandoned the original Boggs challenge — and Dee is being removed from the flight, completing the parallel with Dennis's failure.
jokes.explanation: Superb structural callback. The reveal that Dee ends up in North Dakota — the same exit point as Dennis — is the episode's most elegant piece of construction. It's the perfect mirror: she set out to beat the men but ended up at the same failure point, by the same mechanism (sex and substances). The structure is nearly flawless. High rewatch bonus for fans of the original episode.

jokes.text: One more thing. / Mm... / [Kisses Dee] / Okay. / Bye-bye. Thank you for flying with us.
jokes.setup: The pilot says 'one more thing' as Dee is being removed from the flight
jokes.punchline: The pilot kisses Dee — an unexpected, unexplained, transgressive act — then cheerfully says 'Bye-bye. Thank you for flying with us.' as if it was routine
jokes.explanation: Good final visual gag. The completely unmotivated kiss followed by standard airline pleasantries is genuinely absurdist. No explanation, no reaction, just 'Bye-bye.' Works as a final bit of surreal chaos before the ending.

jokes.text: California, USA.
jokes.setup: Dee has been left in North Dakota while the Waitress continued to L.A.
jokes.punchline: The Waitress made it to California — the character with zero self-preservation instincts and the most catastrophic decisions of the episode (sleeping with Frank) won the challenge.
jokes.explanation: Perfect ironic ending beat — the Waitress, who had sex with Frank and went into a shame spiral, still made it to California while the 'organized' Dee got kicked off in North Dakota. It's a satisfying ironic reversal. 'California, USA' as a two-word victory declaration is excellent economy.

jokes.text: - Meh. - Mmm... [Long silence] / Meh.
jokes.setup: The survivors arrive in California after the whole ordeal
jokes.punchline: Their collective assessment of making it to L.A. after everything is 'meh' — total anti-climax after all the effort
jokes.explanation: Perfect episode-closing beat. The long pause between the two 'mehs' is the joke — the entire episode's effort collapsing into shared indifference. 'Meh' as the final word on a feminist empowerment trip is both funny and thematically resonant. Maximum economy (one syllable), great structure as a final beat.

tmdb_overview: To one-up the guys, Dee has organized an "all-female reboot" of the Wade Boggs challenge on a first-of-its-kind, all-female flight headed to L.A. for the women's march.
